title: Should charities publish what their staff earn?

turns.speaker: Ross
turns.text: The story ran on the chief executive's salary again. A hundred and thirty thousand, and a lot of very angry letters.

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: For an organisation with two thousand staff and a quarter of a billion turnover. That's low for the job, objectively.

turns.speaker: Gwyn
turns.text: The public doesn't compare it to a company that size, though. They compare it to their own wage and to the word charity.

turns.speaker: Ross
turns.text: Which isn't stupid. Donors give assuming the money goes to the cause.

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: And it does, through people who are competent enough to spend it well. Paying badly costs more than it saves in this sector.

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: A bad procurement decision on a fifty million pound programme wipes out the entire salary saving many times over.

turns.speaker: Gwyn
turns.text: The overhead ratio obsession is the underlying problem. Judging a charity by how little it spends on staff rewards starving itself.

turns.speaker: Ross
turns.text: And the ones that publish the lowest overheads are often just accounting it differently.

turns.speaker: Gwyn
turns.text: Frequently. It's the easiest number in the sector to move without changing anything.

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: So the transparency should be about outcomes rather than about inputs.

turns.speaker: Ross
turns.text: Which is much harder to measure and much less satisfying to read.

turns.speaker: Gwyn
turns.text: I'd still publish the salaries, mind you. Not because the number is damning, but because refusing looks worse than any figure would.

turns.speaker: Amara
turns.text: That I'd accept. Publish it and then actually defend it.

points: A charity chief executive's salary of £130,000 prompted public anger despite the organisation's scale.
Amara argues the figure is low for comparable responsibility and that competent management protects funds.
Poor decisions on large programmes can cost far more than any salary saving.
Gwyn identifies the overhead ratio obsession as the underlying problem, rewarding charities that underinvest in staff.
Overhead figures are easily manipulated through accounting rather than actual change.
They agree transparency should focus on outcomes, while still publishing salaries because refusing looks worse than any figure.
